draft.title: Hypothetical RAG Sanity Check: Retrieval-On vs. Retrieval-Off
draft.body: I'm outlining a hypothetical experiment to sanity-check a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) setup. The core idea is to compare a model's responses to a set of questions under two conditions: with retrieval enabled, and with retrieval disabled. This comparison is intended to highlight the impact of the retrieved context. The test corpus would consist of 30 local documents. Crucially, the question set will include queries designed to have no answer within these documents, to observe how the system handles information gaps. It's important to stress that this is a purely hypothetical scenario; no actual measurements or results are available at this stage. The objective is to discuss the design and potential interpretations. What are the key considerations for setting up such a comparison, and how should one interpret the differences in outputs when retrieval is on versus off, especially for unanswerable questions?

draft.title: Designing a Hypothetical RAG Evaluation: Assessing Retrieval Impact
draft.body: This post proposes a hypothetical framework for evaluating RAG system behavior. The central element is a controlled comparison: the same set of questions will be posed to a model, once with its retrieval mechanism active and once with it deactivated. This hypothetical test uses a collection of 30 local documents as the knowledge base. A critical design choice is the inclusion of questions that deliberately lack answers within the provided documents. This aims to test the model's robustness and its reliance on internal knowledge versus retrieved context. Please note, this entire scenario is hypothetical, and no empirical data or measured outcomes exist. The goal is to initiate a technical discussion. What are the primary points to consider when structuring this type of hypothetical RAG evaluation, and how can we best analyze the differences in model outputs when comparing the retrieval-enabled and retrieval-disabled states, particularly for queries that cannot be answered by the corpus?

This experimental setup is purely hypothetical and serves as a thought exercise. No actual performance metrics or accuracy data are available. A key aspect of the question set is the inclusion of queries for which no answer exists within the 30 documents. This is intended to probe the system's behavior when faced with information gaps.
